n: Primary syphilis chancres on the penile shaft

ww.Genital herpes (HSV-2): Genital herpes starts as grouped small vesicles on a red base that burst into clustered, shallow, painful ulcers, often with tender nodes. Chancres are larger, few in number and painless, so pain and a vesicular stage point to herpes.
ww.Chancroid: Chancroid gives a painful, deep ulcer with ragged edges and a gray purulent base, plus a tender node on one side. A painless ulcer with a clean, non-purulent base points away from chancroid and toward a syphilitic chancre.
ww.Granuloma inguinale (donovanosis): Donovanosis forms a beefy-red, velvety ulcer that bleeds on contact and slowly spreads, and biopsy shows Donovan bodies in macrophages. A chancre stays a discrete, round or oval ulcer that does not enlarge into a friable, bleeding plaque.
ww.Lymphogranuloma venereum: Lymphogranuloma venereum begins with a tiny painless papule or ulcer that heals within days, so patients usually present weeks later with painful, matted inguinal buboes. Several persistent, visible ulcers favor syphilis over LGV.

look: Look at the group of moist, shallow, red ulcers on the shaft just behind the glans, which lies at the lower left. They have smooth oval outlines and sharp edges and sit on otherwise intact skin. A painless, sharply demarcated ulcer, usually firm on palpation, that appears about three weeks after exposure is the primary chancre of syphilis, and its serous fluid teems with spirochetes.

findings: Largest chancre, upper right of the shaft: an oval, moist, shallow red ulcer with a sharply defined edge and a smooth base. Its serous surface teems with spirochetes, and a dense plasma cell infiltrate with endarteritis beneath it makes the edge firm on palpation.

Middle chancre, center of the shaft: a second round, moist erosion with a pale center and a red rim. More than one chancre can form when several abraded sites are inoculated, although a single ulcer is more typical.

Lower chancre, below the middle lesion: a further moist, elongated erosion lying on intact surrounding skin. Each lesion marks a site where Treponema pallidum entered, and each heals by itself in weeks even without treatment.

ann.l: This largest chancre is a shallow, red ulcer with a sharply defined edge and smooth base. Its moist surface contains many spirochetes. Histologically, a dense plasma cell infiltrate and obliterative endarteritis in the underlying dermis create the characteristic firm, 'indurated' feel on palpation.

The middle lesion shows a round, moist erosion with a pale center and red rim. While a single painless ulcer is the classic presentation of primary syphilis, multiple chancres can occur if Treponema pallidum is inoculated into several small abrasions simultaneously during sexual contact.

This lower, elongated erosion sits on otherwise healthy-appearing skin. Each of these lesions represents a primary site of bacterial entry. Even without antibiotic treatment, these chancres will typically heal spontaneously within 3 to 6 weeks, though the infection will progress to the secondary stage.
